title: If you yell about everything, you're heard about nothing - a16z crypto
gist: Startup comms in crypto over-uses maximal language on every announcement, which destroys the audience's ability to distinguish real news from routine updates; the piece argues for rationed, selective loudness so that when a company does raise its voice, it actually gets heard.

themes.theme: Attention as a fixed, depletable budget

insights.claim: Audience attention is a fixed budget, and startup comms teams that spend it all at once on every announcement leave nothing in reserve for moments that actually matter.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating a company's PR/IR cadence should treat constant maximal-tone announcements as a signal discount, not a signal amplifier.
insights.quote: The problem is that attention is a fixed budget, and too many players in the industry insist on spending it all at once.
insights.locator: The problem is that attention is a fixed budget

insights.claim: When every message from a company is presented as maximally important, the press and partners lose the ability to rank which updates are genuinely significant versus routine.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Treat a source's inability to distinguish crisis from routine news (because the company cries wolf) as reduced information value from that company's comms.
insights.quote: The press can’t tell what’s important and what’s just a routine Tuesday update. Partners can’t separate a real crisis from reflexive outrage.
insights.locator: The press can’t tell what’s important

themes.theme: Contrast over volume as a positioning strategy

insights.claim: Companies that yell about everything train their audience to default to ignoring them, so that on the day they have genuine news, no one pays attention.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Watch for a credibility cliff: chronically hyperbolic issuers may see muted market/press reaction even to genuinely material news.
insights.quote: The day you have something to say, no one will care. You will have already set your baseline to “ignore.”
insights.locator: Yell about everything, and the people who need to hear you

insights.claim: The loudest, most viral messaging wins short-term engagement metrics but loses the long game of winning over the specific stakeholders (regulators, reporters, institutional partners, long-term customers) who actually drive outcomes.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: For diligence on crypto projects, high social/X engagement is a weak proxy for durable credibility with regulators and institutional counterparties — look for restraint instead.
insights.quote: The loudest take may win the short game — X engagement, virality, a good day on the timeline — but winning the long game means winning over people
insights.locator: Contrast is a more effective way to get

insights.claim: Key long-term stakeholders such as regulators and institutional partners have long memories for companies that habitually cry wolf, which erodes trust over time.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: A track record of exaggerated comms is a durable reputational liability, not a one-off cost — relevant to assessing management credibility over multi-year horizons.
insights.quote: They have long memories for who cried wolf.
insights.locator: They may be regulators, reporters, institutional partners

insights.claim: Companies should ration superlative language like "historic" or "first" for only the events that genuinely qualify, treating such words as a scarce resource.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Frequency of superlative claims in a company's press releases can serve as a quick heuristic for comms discipline and management credibility.
insights.quote: Ration the superlatives. Save “historic” and “first” for things that actually qualify. Spend them like they’re scarce.

insights.claim: In what the article calls the "show-me era," hard traction numbers are more persuasive than adjective-laden press releases.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: When evaluating startup claims, weight disclosed metrics/traction data over narrative language in press releases.
insights.quote: In the show-me era, numbers beat press releases. Traction speaks louder than words.
insights.locator: Let proof do the work adjectives can’t

insights.claim: Companies should selectively choose which negative headlines merit a response rather than reacting to every piece of criticism, since responding to everything achieves nothing.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: A company that responds defensively to every critical article is following a worse comms strategy than one that picks battles — useful lens for reading how a team handles negative press.
insights.quote: Pick your outrage. Not every bad headline deserves a response. Reacting to all of them will get you nowhere. Crybabies don’t win fights.

insights.claim: Maintaining a quiet baseline of communication is what makes genuinely loud moments stand out and register as signal.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Comms cadence itself (quiet baseline vs. constant noise) can be read as a proxy for how much weight to assign a company's next announcement.
insights.quote: Build a quiet baseline. Your loud moments need somewhere to stand out from. Silence gives signal contrast.

insights.claim: In a market where most participants are shouting constantly, the strongest competitive position belongs to those who retain the discipline to discern when it's actually time to speak up.
insights.speaker: Paul Cafiero
insights.so_what: Comms discipline itself can function as a competitive moat/signal in a noisy crypto market — a differentiator worth tracking alongside product and financial metrics.
insights.quote: In a market where everyone is shouting, the most powerful positions belong to those still capable of discerning when it’s time to speak up.
insights.locator: Being loud doesn’t mean being heard
